subject: lion
pitch: A proud old lion resting with his head held high. A huge shaggy mane fading from golden blond at the face to dark chocolate at the edges, a tawny body with a pale cream belly and muzzle, amber eyes, a broad black nose, a scar across one eyebrow, big padded paws and a long tail ending in a dark tuft.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module built with the SDK, thinking through realistic lion proportions for a life-size resting pose—roughly 2 meters long with shoulder height around 1.2 meters, head held high while reclining.

A sphinx-like pose makes the most sense: haunches down, forelegs extended forward, chest lowered, head raised. I'm deciding to construct this with explicit chains and joints rather than IK limbs to keep things reliable, and sketching out coordinates for the hips, spine curve, chest, and neck rising toward a raised head, all facing +Z with the ground at y=0.

For the mane, I'm weighing options — textured cards versus simple colored spikes radiating around the head, favoring spikes for robustness, with color determined by a paint function blending blond near the face to darker chocolate tones toward the edges based on distance from the head center.

I'll use a greyscale SVG strand texture so the paint tint can color it properly, drawing tapered white strand paths with rounded caps, then figure out mane placement by scattering frames around the head on rings at various angles and elevations, with cards leaning outward and slightly back to mimic natural hair flow.

For the head structure, I'm planning a skull sphere with a muzzle attached, a black nose, amber eyes with dark pupils, and a thin dark scar sweep across the brow positioned using local head coordinates for forward/up/right offsets. I'll bind all the mane cards rigidly to the head bone so they move together with the joint.

I'm setting up a jaw joint hinging from the head for a closed-mouth rest pose, then considering small ear shapes and how the mane should wrap around the head while leaving the face region clear—placing mane cards at specific radii and angles so they frame the sides and back without covering the eyes or muzzle.

Now I'm working out the mane generation grid, iterating azimuth and elevation to produce roughly 200+ small card frames filtered to exclude the front face area, then adding jitter and color painting based on each card's distance from the head center in model space.

I'm defining a paint function that blends blond and chocolate tones based on distance from the head, using mix and smoothstep to create a gradient falloff, and planning the strand texture as an SVG with multiple curved strokes.

Writing SVG strand paths...

For stroke width, I'm checking the raster size stays at least 3 pixels so the lines remain visible, and confirming white-to-black textures get tinted by the part's assigned color. Then I'm planning the tail: a catmull-rom chain curving from the hips down to the ground with a dark tuft at the tip, making sure the lowest point still touches the floor.

Now I'm working out the body: tawny back with a cream belly using a countershading function, and sketching the spine as a catmull-rom path from hips to chest with a radius profile that's thicker at the hindquarters. I'm adjusting the hip center height and radius so the haunches actually rest on the ground without floating or clipping below it, trying to get the resting-lion pose proportions right.

Now I'm structuring the joint chains: a root hips joint, a spine chain of three joints running to the chest, and a separate neck chain branching off the spine's last joint up to a forward-tilted head position. I'm figuring out how to sweep a tube through these joint chains with tapering radii for the spine and neck, and countershaded coloring, using the chain object itself as the bone list for the sweep.

For the body I'm defining a simple radius function that thins from hindquarters to chest, keeping a low-poly octagonal cross-section for the stylized look. Then I'm starting to lay out the forelegs in a sphinx pose, with the shoulder angled down-forward into an elbow and forearm resting flat on the ground.

Mirroring the leg path for left and right sides using a sign-based offset, and naming the chain joints shoulder/elbow/wrist/paw so the tip gets its own name too. For the paws I'm placing a flattened, scaled sphere at the tip joint in a darker tawny tone to suggest padded feet.

For the hind legs I'm sketching a folded haunch shape with a big thigh sphere near the hip and a shorter two-span chain down to the hock and paw, keeping the joint-naming convention consistent (names = spans + 1 for the tip). I'm placing another paw sphere at the hind tip and starting the haunch sphere geometry definition now.

Now I'm turning to the head and neck: the head joint sits forward and up near [0, 1.3, 0.66], parented off a short neck chain of two spans whose joints run from around [0, 0.55, 0.3] up to roughly [0, 1.22, 0.6]. I'm adjusting the exact neck path endpoints so the head joint lines up naturally at the top without needing a separate aim direction.

For the skull piece itself I'm deciding between placing a sphere using the head joint's position directly versus using the `frame: head` option, which conveniently inherits both the head's orientation and bone binding at once -- simpler since a sphere is symmetric anyway.

Now I'm working out the muzzle, nose, and jaw: a cream sphere scaled slightly flat for the muzzle sitting forward of the head joint, a black box nose positioned just past the muzzle's front edge, and a lower jaw box attached further down and back to suggest the mouth line, all placed using head-local forward/up offsets.

I'm placing the amber eyes symmetrically using a side-dependent helper that picks left or right offset words depending on which side of the head I'm building.

I'm adding a flattened pupil and considering a scar detail across one brow using a thin pinkish-red rod spanning two nearby points on the head's surface, then moving on to sketch the mane and ear placement.

For the mane, I'm deciding to skip visible ears since the mane covers them, then generating card geometry in layered rings around the head center—sweeping azimuth and elevation angles to compute direction vectors, filtering out the face-facing ones, and placing angled, bent cards at two different radii for a shaggier double-layer effect.

For coloring, I'm computing a gradient based on each card's distance from a point near the front of the face, blending from golden blond near the face to dark chocolate toward the edges using a smoothstep mix, and reusing the same card technique with chocolate tones for the tail tuft.

Now I'm setting up the tail tuft at the tip of the tail chain, placing a ring of frames around that point with upward-leaning directions to create a bushy cluster, and defining the tail's bone chain from hips through several joints down to the tip with a tapering radius.

For color, I'm applying a countershade paint to the body blending tawny and cream, with the tail using color bands that shift from tawny to a darker shade near the tip to blend with the tuft. I'm also considering adding small toe pad details to the paws for extra texture, though keeping them simple.

For the toes, I'm placing small dark spheres offset forward from the paw tip joint using local coordinates, spacing three per paw using a left/right offset, and confirming that the tip joint behaves as a frame I can position relative to.

For the leg geometry, I'm working out the fore leg path points and radii so the paw sphere's bottom sits just barely below the floor within the allowed sink tolerance, tapering the tube radius from shoulder down to wrist so nothing clips awkwardly, then starting to define the hind leg path with similar joint placement for the hock.

Checking the hind leg, I'm making sure the haunch sphere's lower edge sits near the floor without floating oddly, confirming the paws are still the true lowest points, and sweeping the leg tube radius down toward the ankle. I'm also noting the chest and body sphere placements keep their bottoms close to ground level so the silhouette doesn't look disconnected, and confirming the mane cards wrap the neck and lower head region without awkwardly covering the chest.

I'm sizing the mane cards, sketching a strand texture, and building directional frames for each card using spherical coordinates around the head joint so they sit rigidly on the head bone. For jitter, I'm planning to use a seeded random function to add natural variation to the mane card placement.

I'm settling on a color palette for the lion—tawny, cream, blond, dark browns, amber eyes, dark nose and scar tones—then setting up imports for the paint, mix, smoothstep, and svg helper functions needed to shade and texture the model. Writing import statements...

Now I'm structuring the lion's skeleton, starting with a hips joint as the spine root and building out a catmull-rom spline for the spine chain, but I'm catching that placing the spine's first joint at the same position as the hips would create a zero-length bone, so I'm adjusting the coordinates to avoid that overlap.

I'm defining a body sweep over the spine chain with a tapering radius function and slight sine bulge for chest mass, then setting up a neck chain branching off the spine's last joint toward the head position.

Attaching the head joint to the end of the neck chain with its own offset and direction, then setting up a tapered neck sweep with round caps so the tube end blends into the skull sphere. Now I'm starting to lay out the tail chain's path points branching from the hips.

Defining the tail joints and sweep profile with tawny-to-dark color bands and a rounded tip cap, then adding a ring of tuft cards around the tail's final joint using randomized frame positions and upward-leaning directions to fake fur at the tip.

Now I'm setting up the leg chains symmetrically for left and right sides, defining shoulder-elbow-wrist-paw joints along a catmull-rom path, then starting a tapered sweep profile for the foreleg with a forward-narrowing radius function.

Adding paw and toe details...

Writing hind leg chain...

Still placing body parts...

Still positioning eyes and pupils...

Now I'm thinking about adding a brow ridge above the eyes using a dark box shape, and working out whether to attach it via bone or frame so its orientation follows the head's tilt correctly.

For the scar, I'm positioning a small rod across the right eyebrow, but I keep hitting distance mismatches—my candidate endpoints land either slightly inside or outside the skull sphere's radius of 0.2. I'm working toward a cleaner approach: a helper function that normalizes any direction vector and scales it to sit right on the skull's surface, so I can place scar points precisely without manual trial and error.

The scar sits on the right brow area using correct side orientation, and I'm deciding to skip whisker dots and ears for simplicity since the mane would cover them anyway. Now I'm setting up the mane color gradient, blending blond toward chocolate based on distance from the face center.

Writing mane frame placement loop...

Writing SVG strand paths...

Finishing the toe-placement helper, then double-checking that all ground contact points (paws, toes, tail tip) sit near y=0 and the mane covers the chest properly. I'm verifying sweep radius functions all follow the same signature before wrapping up.

Now I'm defining the color palette (tawny, cream, dark, amber, scar tones) and a helper for mirroring left/right side placements, then setting up a head-positioning function to simplify coordinate calls for facial features.

I'm placing a scar across the eyebrow using points computed relative to the skull's surface, tracing a path from above the brow down across the eye, and checking how the rod function accepts its parameters...

Now I'm adding the eyebrow geometry as small boxes positioned relative to the head frame, checking that the eye and brow dimensions overlap naturally, and confirming the frame option types line up correctly before finalizing the mane outline and writing the full code.
